texto_fonte:
PET/CT imaging provides new insights into type 1 diabetes progression
A novel molecular imaging approach that measures beta-cell mass in the pancreas can offer valuable insights into the progression of type 1 diabetes, according to new research published in the Journal of Nuclear Medicine. The study found that individuals who have had type 1 diabetes for less than seven years have higher total beta-cell mass and function, larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat compared to those who have had the disease for longer. This valuable information, paired with functional tests, has the potential to significantly improve clinical trials of new therapeutic interventions.
Globally, more than 9.5 million people live with type 1 diabetes. In this chronic disease, pancreatic beta cells are destroyed over time, leading to an insulin deficiency and thereby hyperglycemia.
"Not all beta cells will be destroyed in type 1 diabetes, but the exact timing and fate of beta-cell loss are still unknown," said Sevilay Tokgöz, Ph.D., a postdoctoral researcher at Radboud University Medical Center in Nijmegen, the Netherlands. "A better understanding of this process is required to develop therapeutic strategies to halt disease progression."
In the study, Tokgöz and colleagues measured total beta-cell mass using ⁶⁸Ga-NODAGA-exendin-4 PET/CT imaging, an approach that targets GLP-1 receptors that are highly expressed on beta cells. Data from 16 individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes (less than seven years) and 10 with long-duration type 1 diabetes (more than seven years) were analyzed. Participants underwent ⁶⁸Ga-NODAGA-exendin-4 PET/CT and a mixed-meal tolerance test to determine total beta-cell mass and function, respectively. Intrapancreatic fat deposition and pancreatic volume were derived from CT.
Total beta-cell mass and function were higher in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with those with long-duration type 1 diabetes. Larger pancreatic volume and lower intrapancreatic fat deposition were also observed in individuals with short-duration type 1 diabetes compared with the long-duration group. Together, these findings provide new insights into the relationship between beta-cell mass, function and disease duration.
"These findings are highly relevant in regard to the development of therapies aimed at restoring beta-cell function or preserving beta-cell mass," said Tokgöz. "They may aid in more precise estimates of treatment effects and improve the logistics of clinical trials, and in the future could identify individuals who may benefit from therapeutic interventions."
Publication details
Sevilay Tokgöz et al., β-Cell Mass and Function, Pancreatic Volume, and Fat Differences Between Short- and Long-Duration Type 1 Diabetes: A Detailed PET/CT Imaging Study, Journal of Nuclear Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.2967/jnumed.126.272915
Journal information: Journal of Nuclear Medicine

candidato.titulo: Evolution's balancing act—keeping genes in sync after genome duplication
candidato.resumo: Getting the right balance is important in all walks of life, whether it's a healthy combination of food groups in a balanced diet or a balanced mix of skills that allows a work or sports team to succeed.

texto_fonte:
Evolution's balancing act—keeping genes in sync after genome duplication
Getting the right balance is important in all walks of life, whether it's a healthy combination of food groups in a balanced diet or a balanced mix of skills that allows a work or sports team to succeed.
Cells face a similar challenge—thousands of genes work together to control cell behavior, and the proteins they produce often need to be present in the correct proportions.
But what happens when the entire genetic code is suddenly doubled, and each copy has the opportunity to evolve independently? How does evolution maintain correct proportions of gene products as individual gene copies evolve and diverge?
A new article by researchers at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences has shed important light on this exact question, indicating that many duplicated genes maintain a connection in how they are regulated, helping to preserve the balance of gene activity across cells. The paper is published in the journal Science Advances.
The dosage-balance challenge after whole-genome duplication
Whole-genome duplication (WGD) is an evolutionary event in which an organism acquires a second copy of its entire genome.
"Ancient WGDs have contributed to the evolution of most eukaryotic life, including humans; we are descendants of two WGDs early in vertebrate evolution," explains the leader of the study, Marie Saitou.
After WGD, all genes have an identical partner, each surrounded by identical DNA sequences that control when, and to what extent, the genes are active. The two gene copies begin with matching sequences and regulatory surroundings, and so the relative proportions of all the proteins encoded by the genes are initially maintained.
However, across millions of years, mutations gradually change the protein-coding potential of genes and their regulation, and some genes even take on new roles or disappear entirely from the genome. This can dramatically impact the dosage balance of protein levels across the cell.
Evolutionary biologists have long been interested in dosage balance theory. Since many proteins do not act alone, but instead as part of large molecular 'teams' in signaling pathways, protein complexes and gene-regulatory networks, evolution may favor mechanisms that help preserve balanced proportions of these proteins.
One way evolution could help maintain such balance after WGD is through dosage compensation.
"Here, a change in activity of one gene copy is offset by an opposing change in the other copy. If one duplicate increases activity, the other becomes less active, helping to stabilize their combined output," says Saitou.
However, the underlying regulatory mechanisms that maintain dosage balance over millions of years following WGD remain poorly understood.
Atlantic salmon as a valuable natural tool to study dosage compensation
Atlantic salmon provide a unique opportunity for studying WGD and dosage compensation, because their lineage experienced WGD relatively recently (80 to 100 million years ago), and many of the duplicated genes are still present today.
In the new study, NMBU researchers used large-scale genomic data from Atlantic salmon to compare genetic variation with differences in gene activity. If a genetic variant correlates with higher or lower activity of a particular gene, this implies that the region where the variant is found plays a role in regulating the activity of the gene in question. Researchers call these regions 'expression quantitative trait loci,' or eQTL.
"Our approach revealed that long-distance regulatory connections were especially common between matching genomic neighborhoods created by genome duplication," explains Célian Diblasi, one of the lead authors of the article.
In other words, many duplicated genes appear not to have evolved entirely independently, but rather to have remained connected through shared regulatory influences that may help to preserve coordinated activity.
This observation was widespread, with a total of 230 duplicated gene pairs sharing an eQTL. Interestingly, a smaller set of 16 gene pairs showed signs of dosage compensation, where an increase or decrease in activity of one copy was matched by a compensatory shift in expression of the other copy.
How evolution preserves balance while creating novelty
These findings shed light on how genome duplication can provide new material for evolution, while preserving regulatory relationships that help maintain the dosage balance of protein-level systems where needed.
The present study implies that, even after 100 million years of divergence, some duplicated genes are still working in concert to maintain this balance.
Diblasi concludes, "Atlantic salmon will continue to provide a valuable tool for researchers studying WGD and its impact on evolution, including our own evolutionary history."
Publication details
Célian Diblasi et al., Evolution of trans-regulatory architecture and gene expression dosage compensation after genome duplication, Science Advances (2026). DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aee6574

texto_fonte:
On 5 November, 10 teams descended upon a 52-acre mock town in College Station, Texas called Disaster City. They were there for a nine-day competition to see how well teams of robots and humans could navigate simulated catastrophes, like a market ravaged by a tornado and a nighttime strike on a military base. At stake? US $2.5 million in prize money.
The scenarios were the final of the DARPA Triage Challenge, which the U.S. agency has been running for three years with the goal of saving more lives in urgent mass casualty events. Engineers from academia and industry have competed in elaborately staged mass casualty events, such as simulated combat zones and plane crash scenes. Teams spent years designing systems where autonomous ground robots and drones could help first responders find mock victims and decide the best way to care for them. “Triage is all about resources,” says Jeremy Pamplin, who managed the challenge for DARPA. Pamplin is a critical care physician and retired colonel who spent 28 years in the U.S. Army.
In mass casualty events, medics race to assess trauma with finite resources and limited time. Some victims need urgent help that medics can provide immediately, like tourniquets to halt bleeding. Some need evacuation and surgery. Others don’t need immediate help—either because their wounds are minimal enough, or because they’re so severe that a medic’s attention is better served elsewhere. Medics must prioritize who gets what care, but the line between each of these scenarios can be murky amid the rubble, frenzy, and heat of the moment.
It’s a difficult problem, and so the technologies developed in this competition could help real-world decisionmaking, says Gabriela Garcia Dolagaray, assistant medical director for emergency preparedness at Massachusetts General Hospital and the Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston. “Finding people can sometimes just be dangerous,” she says, “and getting a robust number of people to go out and search in a disaster area will take time.”
Trauma Technologies and the DARPA Triage Challenge
The Triage Challenge is the latest in a long DARPA legacy of running grand challenges to incentivize proof-of-concept development of important technologies. This particular challenge began as a program to quickly detect signs of trauma. DARPA imagined not only that drones and robots could find casualties, but that machine learning algorithms could assist in triage—which, at its core, is the process of assessing injuries and prioritizing care in a medical emergency.
Pamplin took over the competition in May 2025. “I have friends that still wake up in the middle of the night with these types of recollections and wondering if they did the right thing in the moment during a mass casualty incident,” Pamplin says. “That moves me. I would very much like to eliminate that uncertainty for them to the extent possible with this type of technology.”
He used his experience to make the competition increasingly elaborate and realistic. Year one featured a simulated convoy attack, and human participants sat in protective enclosures to avoid incidental run-ins with robots. In year two, when Pamplin took over the challenge, his team incorporated a full-size airplane fuselage to simulate a plane crash with dozens of victims. Organizers learned to recreate the physical environment of a disaster, and also the physical signs of injuries, like warm blood. Pamplin’s team visited a slaughterhouse with thermal cameras to study the temperature of blood spilling onto the ground. In the competition, they mimic that effect by heating water in a coffee pot and pouring it beside the body. This lets teams detect bleeding even at night.
A man performs a simulated triage as part of DARPA’s Triage Challenge finals. The program was designed to see how robots could assist in making triage decisions during an emergency.Paul Flacks/DARPA
“They always are throwing additional challenging things at us that you wouldn’t expect,” says Sam Colachis, a biomedical engineer at Battelle, an applied science and technology nonprofit in Columbus Ohio who led the organization’s DART team—short for “Drone-Assisted Rapid Triage”—in the competition.
The tactics required for successful triage are inherently multidisciplinary, says Derek Paley, a professor of aerospace engineering leading the University of Maryland’s team, RoboScout. Before 2022, Paley felt confident in his lab’s skills with autonomous navigation and algorithms, but he knew little about trauma medicine. “I didn’t even know what triage was,” he says.
Paley recruited colleagues in emergency medicine to help design his team’s approach and shape their tech. Before the Triage Challenge began, they felt like an underdog. “We kind of have a chip on our shoulder because we think we can play on the same field as these other teams…who’ve done grand challenges before,” Paley told Spectrum before the competition. They finished third in the first year of competition and second last year.
Each year’s competition began with four smaller trials that tested specific components of a robotic system. Teams first released their robots to locate as many casualties (a mix of live actors and manikins) as possible in 15 minutes. Next, they spent five minutes triaging injuries. Another trial presented teams with a fixed number of casualties in known locations to test how they assess trauma. Then, teams had ten minutes to collect vitals like pulse and breathing rate remotely from a few meters away. The top four teams moved into a semi-final where their robots worked with two human medics in simulated emergencies. And the two teams who performed best in four human-machine runs then moved to a 25-minute championship run.
Robots, Drones, and Autonomous Triage
When the teams arrived at Disaster City, they knew very little about the details of what awaited them. One self-funded team of college students from Delhi Technological University flew from India with 22 checked bags, each containing disembodied drones and wheeled robots they had handbuilt. Their team, Unmanned Aerial Systems, learned in the two prior years of the contest to simply expect the unexpected—from DARPA and their own systems. Upon arrival this year, they unzipped their luggage to find broken motors and chassis, camera parts, and missing screws. “We’re still trying to assemble everything before the competition,” Nishant Chandna calmly told IEEE Spectrum a couple days before the challenge. “It’s just part of it.”
Most teams in the challenge designed systems with a mix of ground robots and aerial drones. The student team from India built drones and wheeled robots to search for mock victims with onboard cameras and lidar.
But wheeled robots are problematic. They are more stable, cheaper, and easier to control than legged robots, but they struggle with stairs, entryways, and rough terrain littered with rubble. “We really needed a platform that could traverse those obstacles pretty easily,” says Eric Eaton, a machine learning scientist who led the University of Pennsylvania’s team, which began with drones and wheeled robots before expanding their fleet with four-legged Spot robots from Boston Dynamics that make it up stairs.
Paley’s RoboScout team opted for a strategy that involved sensing the scene from the ground. Their “dogs,” which were also Spot robots, listen for screaming victims, and help in one of the most difficult challenges in autonomous triage: quickly sensing vitals from with thermal cameras and radar. Millimeter-wave radar can detect the subtle movement of a pulse, and thermal cameras can measure breathing rates based on how breathing changes the temperature around a mouth and nose.
Battelle’s team had relied entirely on drones, even for measuring vital signs. Colachis says his team fuses inputs from multiple sensors including thermal, radar, and visual to calculate vitals. The team became almost notorious for their commitment to drones. “They keep threatening to bring a ground robot,” says RoboScout’s Paley, “but they always show up with drones.” For the first two years of the competition, it worked—Battelle won the first two rounds of the competition.
Members of the University of Maryland’s RoboScout team (on right) celebrate a successful run during the DARPA Triage Challenge finals.Paul Flacks/DARPA
RoboScout Wins DARPA Triage Grand Prize
During the final, organizers cast more than 500 actors to simulate casualties throughout the week. DARPA chose these actors to make obstacles like sensing vitals more realistic than previous years. Some were college students instructed to increase their heart and breathing rate on exercise bikes to simulate shock. Endurance athletes were instructed to lower their heart rates, simulating other injuries like airway failures. In the military base simulation, soldiers were running around a compound with alarms blaring. “Some of the explosions caused some of the medics to actually react to it,” Pamplin says, and “pull people to the ground so they didn’t get hit.”
Battelle did finally show up with a ground robot to help with measuring vitals remotely. But this time, the twice-champ finished second. The winner of DARPA’s Triage Challenge grand prize was the RoboScout team from the University of Maryland. The grand prize earned them $1.5 million.
After a perilous start slowed by software errors relating to the competition’s timer and Wi-Fi RoboScout rallied back through the final human-machine teaming portion. “We got hot at the right time,” Paley says. “It was pretty surreal.”
Other teams performed well despite having to improvise through engineering hiccups. Carnegie Mellon’s team, Chiron, struggled with a GPS error. After fixing it, they raced back and nearly made the final. The student team from Delhi didn’t meet a threshold for autonomous control in the competition, but they did earn the highest score in one sub-competition, winning $300,000.
“It’s an incredibly exciting challenge,” says Peter Fischer, trauma medical director with Washington Regional Medical Center in Fayetteville, Arkansas. “We struggle, especially with mass casualty incidents, in determining who the sickest patients are. In trauma, especially, you have to make sure that you triage these patients appropriately, so the sickest ones not only get the care the fastest, but get to the right place at the right time.”
Fischer was intrigued by a non-robotic branch of the competition, where two new teams excelled in predicting urgent care with the help of AI agents. He imagines these advances in robotics and algorithms could connect with additional data from hospitals. Triage algorithms could suggest where to take them to avoid overloading specific hospitals, he says, “That’s where we can really start to make a big difference.”
Although the competition has ended, the work continues. Several participants told IEEE Spectrum they plan to bring their teams’ AI algorithms elsewhere, such as hospital trauma bays, regional medical emergencies, and chemical weapon response.
For his part, DARPA’s Pamplin was most eager to compare performance to human medics without robots. A human-only team located 50 percent of casualties on average in daytime simulations; when paired with medics on one run of the same course, Maryland’s robots found every one. “That was the first time we’ve ever seen that,” he says. In the championship run, humans provided life-saving interventions to 25 percent of the mock casualties who needed them—RoboScout treated 74 percent. “That’s a couple lives,” Pamplin says. “That’s a couple humans that didn’t die that day.”

candidato.titulo: Reitoria da USP recebe secretários estaduais de ciência e tecnologia durante fórum nacional
candidato.resumo: Encontro integrou a programação da "3ª Reunião Anual do Fórum Consecti 2026" e incluiu apresentações institucionais da Universidade, do Instituto Butantan, do IPT e do Ipen

texto_fonte:
Por Michel Sitnik
A Reitoria da USP recebeu, na manhã da terça-feira, 24 de novembro, representantes de secretarias estaduais de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação de diversas regiões do País para um encontro de boas-vindas. O encontro integrou a programação da 3ª Reunião Anual do Fórum Consecti 2026, promovida pelo Conselho Nacional de Secretários Estaduais para Assuntos de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação (Consecti) nos dias 23 e 24 de novembro.
Durante a reunião, os convidados acompanharam apresentações institucionais voltadas ao funcionamento e à articulação de parte do ecossistema científico e tecnológico sediado no entorno do campus do Butantã. Entre as exposições, o reitor Aluisio Augusto Cotrim Segurado detalhou números, dados e estatísticas sobre a Universidade. O diretor do Instituto Butantan, Esper Georges Kallás, e a diretora-superintendente do Instituto de Pesquisas Energéticas e Nucleares (Ipen), Isolda Costa, explicaram detalhes sobre o funcionamento das instituições dirigidas por eles. O presidente do Instituto de Pesquisas Tecnológicas (IPT), Anderson Correia, também dirigiu suas palavras aos presentes, ressaltando que o momento seguinte da programação seria uma visita às instalações da instituição.
“Estas apresentações, de ambientes do ecossistema de ciência, tecnologia e inovação do Estado de São Paulo, que nos rodeiam, dão um panorama geral de como estamos e de como temos buscado integrações potencializadoras, valendo-nos das instalações e da qualidade do pessoal vinculado a cada uma das instituições representadas, buscando, com essas parcerias, dar à sociedade paulista e brasileira o melhor que podemos”, comentou o reitor.
O grupo contou também com a participação da vice-reitora da USP, Liedi Légi Bariani Bernucci; do secretário de Ciência, Tecnologia e Inovação do Estado de São Paulo, Vahan Agopyan; e do chefe de gabinete da Reitoria, Edmilson Dias de Freitas.
Agenda de dois dias na Cidade Universitária
O encontro na Reitoria fez parte de uma programação de dois dias que aproximou universidades, governos e gestores de ciência, tecnologia e inovação de todo o País. Formado pelos 27 secretários estaduais da área, o Consecti atua na integração de políticas públicas, na cooperação entre os governos estaduais e federal e na articulação com universidades, instituições de pesquisa e agências de fomento.
Voltada a secretários, gestores públicos, representantes de instituições científicas e consulados, a reunião anual tratou de temas de interesse compartilhado com a USP, como o financiamento da pesquisa científica e tecnológica, o fortalecimento das fundações estaduais de amparo à pesquisa, a cooperação entre universidades, empresas e governos e a formação de pesquisadores. As atividades incluíram o debate Segurança jurídica para a inovação no setor público: como transformar boas ideias em políticas públicas efetivas, uma plenária de discussão e uma visita técnica ao IPT.

candidato.titulo: 7 new Intel Nova Lake-S Core Ultra 4000-series CPUs detailed in new leak
candidato.resumo: A number of new, unannounced Intel Core Ultra 4000-series chips have been detailed in a Nova Lake document, ahead of what is expected to be an official unveiling of the chips at a next-generation desktop chip event in Berlin, Germany, in February 2027.

texto_fonte:
A newly leaked document purportedly details no less than seven new Nova Lake-S desktop processors based on C1 stepping qualification samples, including 28-core models, three months before Intel is expected to officially take the wraps off them. The new leak, from VideoCardz, includes an Intel warning that clock speeds and performance may change before the final products are ready to be shipped. But given the fact that this rarely happens when dealing with qualification samples, it's believed that the chips will likely be released just as they are outlined in the document, if the leak is accurate.
Of the seven chips that have been detailed, the top-of-the-line Core Ultra 9 4970K BFC will be the one of most interest. It will reportedly feature 28 cores comprising eight performance cores, 16 efficiency cores, and four low-power efficient cores. Its base efficiency core clock speed of 2.7 GHz is eclipsed by the 5.5 GHz boost speed its performance cores will reach, while 144 MB of L3 cache and a 125-watt power rating round out the main figures. According to the leak, it will be joined by a Core Ultra 9 4950K with the same core count and almost identical clock speeds, albeit with a much smaller 36 MB L3 cache. Beyond that, the report says the Core 9 4900 BFC will be locked at 65 watts, have 22 cores, and a 120 MB L3 cache.
If the leak holds up, the mid-range will be catered for by the Core Ultra 7 4870K and 4850K chips. Both will reportedly have a 125-watt power rating and 24 cores, but will again differ in terms of L3 cache — the former will have 144 MB, the latter just 36 MB. Both will boost to 5.2 GHz.
The report says the entry-level models will include the Core Ultra 5 4650K and 4650KF, both packing 22 cores and 30 MB L3 caches, and that they'll also have the same 125-watt power rating and top out at a boosted 5.1 GHz, according to the documentation.
The document reportedly states that all seven processors will support DDR5-8000 RAM, an increase over the DDR5-6400 that the Arrow Lake-S chips top out at. The specs also indicate a maximum of 256 GB of RAM is supported, with 24 CPU PCIe lanes and a 77 PTOPS integrated NPU. Integrated graphics are set to range from 2.9 to 3.1 GHz depending on the chosen chip, with support for the DNx, XAVC, JPEG-XS, and VVC decoding all included alongside AV1 High and Professional profile support.
It has previously been reported that Intel is likely to announce its next-gen chips at an event in Berlin, Germany, between February 22 and 25, 2026. But we can also expect that motherboard manufacturers will show off products compatible with the new chips before that — no doubt at the CES 2027 event in Las Vegas in January. It's already been confirmed that new motherboards will be needed if you plan on picking up any of the next-gen chips.
This latest leak comes weeks after it was reported that the new Nova Lake chips would "universally limit the maximum core frequency to 5.1 GHz when above 90°C." However, it's important to remember that the limitation only applies when the chips reach that temperature. Machines with adequate cooling will not experience that limitation, although it remains to be seen how easy these chips are to cool.

candidato.titulo: NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman
candidato.resumo: These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

texto_fonte:
An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.
Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find new planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.
Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.
Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.
A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.
Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (#17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- IQM Quantum Computers has secured an order from South Korean company QAI for an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer to be installed at QAI’s data centre in Seoul.
- The system is expected to be delivered by the end of 2027 and will be the first IQM quantum computer deployed in a private data centre in Asia.
- QAI plans to offer access through its Quantum-as-a-Service platform, combining quantum computing resources with GPU-based infrastructure for enterprise, research and public-sector customers.
PRESS RELEASE — IQM Quantum Computers (Nasdaq: IQMX), a global leader in superconducting quantum computers, is partnering with QAI Co., Ltd., a South Korean quantum-AI data center and cloud infrastructure company, to deliver an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer. The order covers a complete on-premises quantum computing solution for QAI’s data center, including an IQM Radiance R3 system and associated services.
The 54-qubit quantum computer will be the first IQM quantum computer deployed to a private data center in Asia. The deal brings on-premises quantum computing into QAI’s commercial data center environment, where it will help build applications and a resilient, competitive infrastructure within South Korea’s quantum ecosystem. The IQM Radiance R3 is expected to be delivered and installed on-premises at QAI’s data center in Seoul by the end of 2027.
“We are proud to partner with QAI as they bring an IQM Radiance R3 54-qubit quantum computer to their data center in Seoul,” said Sylwia Barthel de Weydenthal, Chief Commercial Officer at IQM Quantum Computers. “This sale marks an important milestone for quantum computing in South Korea. With on-premises access to IQM Radiance, QAI will be able to accelerate research, develop commercial applications for businesses and support sovereign quantum capabilities that keep critical technology and data under national control. We look forward to working closely with QAI to build a thriving quantum ecosystem in Korea and across the Asia-Pacific region.”
QAI builds data centers that combine GPU-based AI computing with quantum computing resources. Once the system is operational, QAI plans to make it available to its customers through its Quantum-as-a-Service (QaaS) offering. This would give Korean enterprises, research institutions and public organizations access to the IQM Radiance R3 quantum computer hosted in South Korea. The system will initially be used to explore industry use cases in compute-intensive fields such as drug discovery, next-generation materials, including batteries, financial portfolio optimization and scheduling optimization for logistics and energy infrastructure.
“By bringing IQM Radiance R3 into our data center in Seoul, we are creating a place where Korean companies and researchers can use GPUs and a quantum computer together to solve real problems,” said Ui-tae Kim, Co-CEO and CTO of QAI. “Together with IQM, we will build an environment where Korea’s industry and research community can work with quantum computing hands-on.”
IQM Radiance is IQM’s most powerful on-premises quantum computer, designed for integration into high-performance computing (HPC) environments, where installing it on site reduces latency for hybrid quantum-classical workloads. The 54-qubit system offers high-fidelity gates and tunable couplers between the qubits, arranged in a square lattice with the highest connectivity available at this scale. Its layout natively supports surface-code error correction. Customers own and operate the system on site, with pulse-level access and the option to upgrade with the latest chips and components as IQM’s technology develops.
South Korea has made quantum technology a national priority. Under its Sixth Basic Plan for Science and Technology, the government plans to invest more than 200 trillion South Korean won (approximately EUR 135 billion) in research and development between 2026 and 2030, with quantum named as one of ten national strategic technology fields. In January 2026, the Ministry of Science and ICT also set out its first comprehensive plan for the quantum science, technology and industry, which aims to give Korea the world’s highest utilization rate of quantum computers by 2035, alongside training 10,000 quantum professionals and fostering 2,000 quantum companies. Reaching those goals will require businesses and researchers in Korea to have hands-on access to quantum computers. With IQM‘s quantum computer installed on-premises and integrated into its data center offering, QAI will be able to provide that access as a service to customers across Korea.
IQM‘s first quantum computer in South Korea, an IQM Spark at Chungbuk National University, was the first commercial quantum computer installed through the Korean government’s official procurement process. IQM opened its Seoul office in June 2025. The QAI order will further extend IQM’s installed base across Asia-Pacific, following systems already delivered in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan.

By now, the importance of backing up your Windows PC or laptop goes without saying. Just take a moment to consider how much of your data is at potential risk of a drive failure, natural disaster, or a bad actor, if you don’t have a solid backup plan in place. The best Windows backup software includes file backup, sure, but also disk imaging and full image restore, as well as disaster recovery.
Our picks for best Windows backup software are selected with all the must-haves of data backup and recovery in mind, so in the tragic event that your primary local data repository is compromised, you’re fully covered.
At a glance
What backup utilities come with Windows?
Sadly, while other operating systems make backup easy, Microsoft saddles users with a patchwork system of utilities and holdover imaging tools from Windows 7.
Some of these work well (Restore Points, File History), others don’t (System Repair Disc, Recovery Drive). None are suitable for quick and easy disaster recovery — even the online backup that is available when you use Windows with a Microsoft cloud account.
Thankfully, there are a number of highly capable and far more reliable third-party backup options for Windows that cover the panoply of backup, restore, migration, and disaster recovery.
Why you should trust PCWorld for backup software reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name — PCWorld. Our reviewers have been testing PC hardware, software, and services for decades. Our backup evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the promises and limitations of every product — from performance to the practicalities of regular use.

Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX: Further considerations

ShadowProtect SPX is a bit pricey, but it’s extremely reliable backup software with foolproof continuous data protection. Note that the company no longer targets the average user, but I found that it works exceptionally well even on a single computer.
Read our full Arcserve ShadowProtect SPX Desktop review
Other notable Windows backup software
- Handy Backup Professional: Top-notch features that might’ve garnered a higher rating had it been entirely glitch-free and a bit easier to learn.
- NTI Backup Now Pro 7: Another suite that offers a strong feature set — file backup, imaging, continuous and cloud backup — yet is tarnished by glitches.
- Ashampoo Backup Pro 27: A great total backup solution for the average user, but a couple features shy of being “pro.”
- Paragon Backup & Recovery Community Edition: A free program that offers robust file backup that should meet the needs of most users.
- Perfect Backup: Fast and competent, this free backup program is more versatile than Windows File History.
- Aomei Backupper Pro: A complete backup solution capable of preserving your important data both locally and remotely.
- Aomei Backupper Standard: A respectable free backup program if you can tolerate the occasional ad.
- Retrospect 19 Solo: Includes support for both proprietary and third-party cloud storage, but sadly it lacks disaster recovery.
- Retrospect 19 Desktop: The pro version of the above covers all the bases, but has a steep learning curve and high price.
- Backup and Restore (Windows 7): Conveniently installed with Windows, and good for imaging but bad for disaster recover.
- MSP360 Managed Backup: Uses a handy web-based console to provide imaging and file backup services for multiple devices at a reasonable price.
- MSP360 Backup: The free incarnation is a worthwhile upgrade to Windows File History.
- Iperius Backup: Has power aplenty, but the learning curve and interface might occasionally flummox less-experienced users.
- MiniTool ShadowMaker Pro 4.6: There’s a lot to like, particularly its unique ability to interface with all computers on a network.
- Macrium Reflect Home: Would likely qualify as our favorite backup software if it wasn’t relatively pricey. It’s an exceptional program that offers everything we want from backup software — full drive/folder backup, ease of use, reliability, etc.
- DriveImage XML: A viable free backup solution, albeit only for MBR disks.
Note that in this article we focus on local-software based solutions, although many also include a cloud component. For cloud-first backup, see our roundup of the best online backup services. Admittedly, the distinction between the two categories is blurring as they each expand their feature sets.
How we test
Our reviewers run each program through the various types of backups and restores it’s capable of — including those requiring boot media. This is largely to gauge reliability and hardware compatibility. We check speed, but such is highly reliant upon the connections and media involved.
If we notice anything is particularly fast or slow, we’ll tell you about it, but creating a functional backup is paramount.
To learn more details, see our article on how PCWorld tests backup software.
Who curated this article
Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two.
How to choose backup software
If you recently purchased an external HDD or SSD from a major vendor such as Seagate or WD, check to see if there are backup utilities or a backup software license included. Whatever backup software you use, keep in mind the following key aspects of the best solutions: file backup for documents/photos, image backup for whole-PC rollback, boot media for dead-drive recovery, versioning for accidental overwrite protection, and know which are critical to your backup plan.
File backup
If you want to back up your essential data (operating systems and programs can be reinstalled, though it’s mildly time- and effort-consuming), a program that backs up only your important files is essential. Some programs even automatically select the appropriate files or folders. File backup can include operating system files if you wish but is still not suitable for disaster recovery.
Image backup/imaging
Images are byte-for-byte snapshots of your entire hard drive (normally not including empty sectors) or partitions, and can be used to restore the operating system, drivers, programs in one swift, fell swoop. Imaging also ensures that you don’t omit anything important as can happen with file backup.
Recovery boot media
Should your system crash completely, you need alternate means to boot your system and restore data using your backup software. Any backup program worth its salt should be able to create a bootable optical disc or USB thumb drive. Some will also create a restore partition on your hard drive, which can be used if the issue isn’t a failed drive.
Note that we’ve run into multiple issues with Microsoft’s own Recovery Drive and System repair disc — don’t rely on those.
Scheduling
If you’re going to back up effectively, you need to do so on a regular basis. Any backup program you purchase should let you schedule backups and run them in the background. Some even will backup files as they change (real time) or at very short intervals (continuous)
Versioning
Versioning is simply retaining older version of files (or backups) rather than overwriting them during the backup/sync process. You can generally define how many versions to keep, but if you choose to cull older files, this is till not true backup which again, is an immutable copy of your data, drives, or system.
Optical discs
Every backup program supports hard drives, but as obsolete as they may seem, DVDs and Blu-Ray discs are great archive media. If you’re worried about optical media’s reliability, M-Disc claims its discs are reliable for a thousand years, backed up by Department of Defense testing.
Online storage (cloud) support
An offsite copy of your data is a hedge against physical disasters such as theft, flood, fire, and power surges. Online storage services are a great way to meet that need. Some backup software will let you back up to Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, Amazon S3 and compatible, etc. however Cloud Managers can serve as a workaround with backup programs that don’t. The downside to cloud storage is relatively slow performance. Keep a local backup for faster restores.
Network access
Backing up to other computers or NAS boxes on your network or in remote locations (say your parent’s or children’s house) is another way of safeguarding your data via a physically remote copy. If you use network storage, it can also be handy to back them up to you local system.
FTP/SFTP can be used for offsite, while SMB (Windows and most OS’s) and AFP (Apple) are good for other PCs or NAS on your local network. Network support is not universal, and some backup programs allow you to back up to, but not from network shares. Just be careful in the way you expose your computers on the Internet.
Real-time backup
Real-time backup means that files are backed up whenever they change, usually upon creation or save. It’s handy for keeping an immediately available backup of rapidly changing data sets. For less volatile data sets, scheduled backups will do just fine.
Continuous backup
Continuous simply means backing up on a tight schedule, generally every few minutes, rather than in real time, daily, weekly, or monthly. Use continuous backup for rapidly changing data sets where transfer rates are too slow, or computing power too precious for real-time backup.
Performance concerns
Most backups proceed in the background or during dead time, so performance isn’t a huge issue in the consumer space. However, if you’re backing up multiple machines, backing up to multiple destinations, or dealing with very large data sets, speed will be a consideration. That said, backup speed is highly dependent upon the hardware and transport technology in use.
Further reading: Check out PCWorld’s roundup of best external drives for recommendations on reliable storage options — an important component in a comprehensive backup strategy.
FAQ
What is the best Windows backup software?
The best Windows backup software is Easeus Todo Backup 2025. It has everything PCWorld expects to see in a top product: A polished interface, intuitive functionality, a comprehensive approach to backing up data including imaging, file backup, sync, and disaster recovery. And most important, it’s reliable! Todo Backup also offers the option of a perpetual license or a subscription model, the latter of which can be augmented with affordable cloud storage.
What is the best free Windows backup software?
It turns out that PCWorld’s favorite for-pay backup software, Easeus Todo Backup 2025, also offers a surprisingly robust free version. It matches its paid counterpart in basics such as imaging, file backup, sync, and, most especially — disaster recovery. It also features the same eminently user-friendly interface. As with most backup freeware, you will be nagged to upgrade, and Easeus’s optional cloud storage, which is surprisingly affordable, is only available at the subscription tier.
Will backup software slow down my computer?
Backup software typically runs in the background or during dead time, so given even moderately modern hardware, you shouldn’t notice any decrease in performance. Most programs let you throttle the backup process if you do notice a slowdown.
Does Windows Backup and Restore (Windows 7) save everything?
Yes, by default, Backup and Restore (Windows 7) saves everything on your system disk (all the partitions, including hidden ones) in what’s known as an image file that would be suitable for disaster recovery if Windows Recovery Drive and Rescue disk were reliable. News bulletin — they aren’t.
Hence, we only recommend this program for creating highly compatible VHD/VHDX images of your data drives and partitions which can be mounted as virtual drives and browsed using nothing but Windows Explorer.
What’s the difference between Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, etc. and backup software?
Google Drive, Dropbox, and OneDrive are what’s known as cloud storage, or online storage. They create a local virtual drive that you can drag files to, and which is eventually synced to the cloud as time allows. They also provide a Web portal where you can manage your files remotely.
However, by default these services sync changes in the data across all devices. True backups should be immutable snapshots that may be added to but not changed. Some services offer versioning (keeping older files, and adding new ones), which creates a close approximation to backup.
Cloud backup services (distinct from those mentioned above) offer many, though not all, of the benefits of Windows backup software. This is generally done with local client software that offers just basic functions like file backup and sync. You can learn more about these in our roundup of best cloud backup services.
How often should backups be scheduled?
Ideally, as often as your data changes. If you are working on an important project or have work that you absolutely cannot afford to lose, you should consider real time (as data changes) or continuous (very short intervals). Hourly, daily, or longer intervals will be fine for the average user. All file backups should be augmented by weekly or monthly system backups.
Can I back up files to and from my cloud storage?
Until a few years ago, most Windows backup software was restricted to making local backups — i.e., to another drive, external or internal, connected to your system. There were of course services such as Mozy that had their own backup clients, but that’s covered in our online backup roundup. Here we’re talking just plain backup programs.
The situation is improving rapidly, and many backup software vendors are adding online storage services as destinations for their backups.
If your favorite backup program doesn’t support cloud storage directly, a cloud storage manager that integrates online storage services into File Explorer can make online backup possible with just about any backup app.
What’s the difference between full, differential, and incremental backup?
A full backup is a backup of all your data, regardless of how new or old it is. A differential backup is all the data that’s changed since your last full backup. An incremental backup is all the data that’s changed since any your original full and/or the last differential/incremental backup. Differential and incremental backups require a initial full backup to be restored.
Differential backups require more time to create than incremental backups, but are quicker to restore since you only need the latest iteration. Differential backups can grow to be quite large if you don’t perform full backups very often.
Incremental backups take less time to produce and are smaller, but take longer to restore as all of them created since the last full backup must be restored in the order in which they were created.
What’s the difference between image backup, system backup, and file backup?
An image is low-level backup of all the sectors (including “empty” sectors if you wish) contained by a disk or partition, regardless of their pertinence to your files. It’s basically fool-proof in terms of accidentally overlooking important data.
A system backup is an disk image backup of all the partitions on your system drive. This includes several that are hidden, i.e., not enumerated as drive letters by the operating system. A system backup might also include other drives, but must contain the OS drive.
A file backup is a high-level backup of data read via the operating system’s file system. Most often this is data, but may include all the files on a drive.
What should I back up?
In truth, it’s only your essential personal data that must absolutely, positively, 100% be backed up. Once the family pictures or your work-in-progress are trashed with no backup, there’s no way back other than an expensive recovery service, and even that’s not guaranteed if the physical media is unreadable.
On the other hand, a system backup is exceedingly handy for getting you back up to speed with minimal hassle. It returns your system to exactly where you were at the time of the backup: OS, program, updates, upgrades, settings, data are all back in a relative blink of the eye.
But it’s not essential. While reinstalling operating systems, drivers, and programs, as well as adjusting settings require more effort, you can then recover your data if that’s all you backed up. See the first paragraph.

One UI 9.5 vai ganhar recurso de IA que melhora fotos com zoom no celular
Por Marcelo Fischer |
A Samsung está desenvolvendo uma ferramenta de inteligência artificial (IA) capaz de melhorar a qualidade de fotografias tiradas com zoom nos celulares Galaxy. O “Zoom Enhancer” permitirá aprimorar a nitidez de imagens diretamente na Galeria do celular, mesmo após a captura.
A novidade foi identificada pelo SamMobile nesta quarta-feira (25) na primeira versão beta da One UI 9.5 para a linha Galaxy S26.
A ferramenta ainda está oculta no sistema e não pode ser acessada pelos participantes do programa de testes.
Como funciona o Zoom Enhancer da Samsung?
Diferentemente do zoom óptico, que utiliza as lentes da câmera para aproximar uma cena, o zoom digital recorta e amplia uma parte da imagem capturada pelo sensor. Esse processo pode resultar na perda de detalhes e na redução da nitidez da fotografia.
O Zoom Enhancer utilizará o Galaxy AI para aprimorar tanto fotos tiradas com altos níveis de zoom quanto imagens de baixa resolução.
Após ativar o recurso nas configurações da Galeria, o aplicativo deverá identificar automaticamente fotografias que podem ser aprimoradas e sugerir a edição.
Nos exemplos divulgados pelo SamMobile, a ferramenta conseguiu reduzir os ruídos presentes na fotografia, mas apresentou uma melhora pouco significativa no nível de detalhes.
A própria Samsung alerta que os detalhes gerados pela IA podem ser diferentes daqueles presentes na cena original. Isso significa que a ferramenta pode recriar elementos e texturas que não foram registrados com precisão pela câmera.
Após o processamento, será possível comparar a imagem original com a versão aprimorada, salvar o resultado na Galeria ou compartilhá-lo.
O Android Authority também identificou que a ferramenta depende do processamento em nuvem. Segundo informações encontradas na interface do recurso, a Samsung não armazenará as imagens processadas em seus servidores.
Zoom Enhancer será um recurso pago?
A Samsung está desenvolvendo uma possível assinatura chamada Galaxy AI Premium, que deverá oferecer ferramentas mais avançadas de inteligência artificial e limites maiores de utilização.
A fabricante já informou que os recursos básicos do Galaxy AI continuarão gratuitos, mas que novas funcionalidades poderão ser pagas. Ainda não há confirmação de que o Zoom Enhancer fará parte da assinatura.
One UI 9.5 terá novidades na câmera
Além do Zoom Enhancer, outras ferramentas relacionadas à fotografia foram anunciadas ou identificadas na nova versão do sistema:
- Reformulação do aplicativo Câmera, com botões maiores e configurações personalizáveis nos modos Pro e Vídeo Pro;
- Captura de fotografias panorâmicas de até 360 graus, utilizando as câmeras frontal e traseira do celular;
- Criação de vídeos curtos com IA, a partir de fotos e vídeos armazenados na Galeria.
A One UI 9.5 está em fase beta em seis países, e o Brasil ainda não faz parte do programa de testes. A expectativa é que a versão estável seja lançada no início de 2027, junto à linha Galaxy S27.

texto_fonte:
Wolf pack approach to wind and solar power
Researchers have developed a new way of managing electricity supplies that could help keep power grids stable as they become more dependent on wind and solar energy. Details of the algorithmic approach, which is based on the hunting behavior of a wolf pack, are reported in the International Journal of Critical Infrastructures.
The growing use of renewable energy is a challenge to power infrastructure because wind and sunlight are unpredictable. Electricity generation can rise and fall quickly, making it harder to balance supply with demand. This can cause changes in the grid's frequency, a measure of the stability of the electricity supply.
The study offers a new approach to managing these fluctuations. It estimates how much support renewable sources can reliably provide before distributing instructions to thermal power stations, telling them how much to increase or reduce their output.
In tests, the method reduced frequency fluctuations to 0.11 hertz. It also achieved a maximum of over 87% reduction in renewable energy fluctuations. It was able to work out the instructions in under 0.4 seconds.
The findings could help electricity networks incorporate more wind and solar power by making better use of existing power stations to compensate for unpredictable changes in renewable generation.
Publication details
Huaguo Shao et al., An adaptive allocation strategy of thermal power frequency regulation instructions for high proportion new energy grids, International Journal of Critical Infrastructures (2026). DOI: 10.1504/ijcis.2026.157706

candidato.titulo: Encontro aberto na USP em Pirassununga apresenta soluções para o saneamento
candidato.resumo: Evento desta sexta-feira, 27 de novembro, reúne pesquisadores, estudantes e o serviço municipal de água e esgoto para apresentar tecnologias de monitoramento da água e prevenção de vazamentos

texto_fonte:
.
A USP em Pirassununga recebe nesta sexta-feira, 27 de novembro, a primeira edição do CEHIGERA para a Comunidade, encontro aberto ao público que vai apresentar pesquisas e tecnologias voltadas ao saneamento e à sustentabilidade dos recursos hídricos. A programação começa às 8h30, com um café de recepção no Anfiteatro do Prédio Central do campus.
Depois da abertura, pesquisadores do Centro de Pesquisa Aplicada em Sustentabilidade Hídrica e Gestão de Recursos Ambientais (CEHIGERA) vão apresentar as linhas de pesquisa do grupo. Na sequência, o Serviço de Água e Esgoto de Pirassununga (SAEP) vai expor desafios do saneamento no município e mostrar exemplos de soluções que podem ser adotadas por serviços de água e esgoto de outras cidades.
O encontro termina com a apresentação de pôsteres científicos pelos estudantes e um momento de conversa com o público. A proposta é aproximar a universidade da comunidade e discutir como as pesquisas podem ajudar a enfrentar problemas do abastecimento de água e do tratamento de esgoto.
Centro testa tecnologias de baixo custo no saneamento municipal
Vinculado à Faculdade de Zootecnia e Engenharia de Alimentos (FZEA) da USP, o CEHIGERA é um Centro de Ciência para o Desenvolvimento financiado pela Fundação de Amparo à Pesquisa do Estado de São Paulo (Fapesp). Reúne pesquisadores e estudantes de pós-graduação de áreas como materiais, química, física, inteligência artificial e engenharia agronômica. Na FZEA, participam equipes de Zootecnia, Medicina Veterinária, Engenharia de Biossistemas e Engenharia de Alimentos.
As pesquisas abrangem a captação de água e a conservação dos mananciais, o tratamento e o monitoramento da água, a redistribuição e o reúso, o tratamento de esgoto e o manejo de rejeitos. “Pesquisamos, desenvolvemos e entregamos soluções para os problemas identificados”, diz o professor Ernane José Xavier Costa, coordenador do Centro.
Uma dessas soluções surgiu de uma demanda do serviço municipal de Pirassununga relacionada a vazamentos. A equipe desenvolveu e colocou em operação um protótipo de baixo custo para monitorar o nível da água nos reservatórios, com pedido de patente feito em parceria com o SAEP. Um sistema de previsão de vazamentos também está em uso. Segundo o Centro, o monitoramento implantado no município reduziu em quase 93% o custo em relação à contratação de serviços de terceiros.
Costa cita o exemplo de um sensor comercial de R$ 100 mil para explicar a estratégia da equipe. Ao desenvolver um sensor específico para a aplicação, o objetivo é reduzir o custo para R$ 1 mil. O serviço municipal funciona como campo de testes em condições reais, e, segundo o professor, outras empresas já demonstraram interesse nas tecnologias. O Centro também pretende firmar parcerias com serviços de saneamento de outros municípios.
.
Inteligência artificial e energia para sensores
Entre os projetos em desenvolvimento estão o processamento digital de sinais e imagens aplicado à segurança hídrica e um biossensor virtual que usa inteligência artificial para estimar, em estações de tratamento de água, riscos de efeitos cancerígenos e de danos ao fígado. O grupo também estuda o uso de organismos vivos para auxiliar no monitoramento ambiental.
Outra linha de pesquisa busca gerar eletricidade no próprio local onde os sensores operam. Em parceria com a empresa holandesa Plant-e, o Centro pretende testar, em áreas de captação de água, uma tecnologia que usa plantas para gerar energia e alimentar sensores. Uma segunda frente estuda o aproveitamento de rejeitos do esgoto por meio de células a combustível microbianas, que utilizam bactérias capazes de gerar corrente elétrica.
O Centro também mantém parcerias com a Universidade de Nevada e o Fórum Animal, organização de proteção animal. Segundo Costa, a equipe já captou recursos externos além do financiamento inicial da Fapesp. Entre os desafios desta fase estão a formação de uma equipe de gestão e a ampliação do quadro de pesquisadores e profissionais. O Centro busca contribuir para os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável e, segundo o coordenador, considera a diversidade de gênero e a inclusão de pessoas pretas, pardas, indígenas e de outros grupos sub-representados na formação da equipe.
